verdict.reasoning: Patient reports 'soreness in my fingers' and that 'the skin on my hands is kind of cracked' and later confirms itchiness: 'yeah, it does get itchy.'
Duration and symptoms are stated: 'A couple of months ago. Like, three, four months ago.' and she has hand soreness and cracked skin. Gradual onset is implied over months without an acute start.
Worsening and work impact: Doctor asks if she came because it got worse; patient: 'Yeah, I mean, it's gotten to a point where it hurts a lot, and I can't really do my job.'
Location: Doctor: 'Which part of your hands are affected? Mainly the palm.' This establishes that symptoms mainly affect the palms.
Itching is intermittent: Doctor: 'Have you noticed any itchiness in your palms?' Patient: 'Yeah, it's itchy. Not all the time, but, yeah, it does get itchy.'
Bleeding with scratching: Doctor asks about bleeding; patient: 'when I scratched it, yes, it has bled sometimes, but... otherwise it hasn't bled on its own.'
Treatments tried: Patient: 'Yeah, I've tried E45.' and 'I was trying antihistamines... But it didn't.' Doctor confirms E45 'didn't really do anything.'
Time off work: Doctor: 'Have you had to take time off work recently?' Patient: 'Yeah, like the past three days, I haven't been able to go to work.'
Job change timing: Patient: 'I switched jobs four months ago. I've been working for... as a housekeeper for a while though.' This matches approximately 4 months.
Past medical history: Doctor: 'do you have any other conditions at all?' Patient: 'I have diabetes.'
Medication: Doctor: 'Which medication do you take?' Patient: 'Metformin.' This is clearly for her diabetes contextually.
The transcript does not address changing or continuing diabetes therapy; metformin is only listed as current medication. No explicit plan regarding diabetes management is mentioned.
Family history: Doctor: 'Family history wise? Is there anything I should be aware of?' Patient: 'Diabetes as well?' Doctor repeats: 'Diabetes as well?' Patient: 'Yes.'
Occupation: Patient: 'I do work as a housekeeper.' and later clarifies work location as 'It's a hotel.'

Cleaning agents and glove use: Patient: 'to be honest, I'm not always very good about wearing gloves' and later: 'Yeah, I usually use [cleaning products] for bathrooms, but, yeah, bedrooms and corridors. Not always.'
Smoking: Doctor: 'Do you smoke at all?' Patient: 'No.'
Alcohol: Doctor: 'Do you drink much in the way of alcohol?' Patient: 'Once a week. A couple of pints.' Doctor summarizes: 'A week. Okay, so very minimal alcohol there.'

Assessment: Doctor: 'you might have something called dermatitis or contact dermatitis' of the hands; earlier discussion describes pain, cracked skin, and impact on work: 'it hurts a lot, and I can't really do my job.' 'Cracked' implies fissuring.

Occupational relation: Doctor links it to cleaning products and glove use: 'particularly people in your field who are using cleaning products, not using gloves... get a bit of a reaction between the chemicals and your skin.'
While diabetes is noted, there is no statement that it 'may affect skin healing' or that this effect is considered in the assessment.
Glove advice: 'what we try and do is avoid the trigger. So in your case, I strongly recommend that you wear gloves when cleaning at all times.'
Topical steroid: 'we can try some steroid creams to help with inflammation.'
Emollients: 'as well as some stronger emollients which you really need to kind of coat on throughout the day.'
Frequency: 'throughout the day, three, four times a day for the next couple of weeks.'
Prescription destination: 'So I'll do a prescription for you now and send over to your pharmacy.'

Follow-up timeframe: 'If it still hasn't got better in about a week to two weeks time, I really want you to come back and see me again' and later clarifies 'a minimum couple of weeks, 10 days to 14 days.'
Return sooner if worse: 'if it still hasn't got better, or indeed if it's getting worse, if it's spreading or dryness is getting worse, come back and see me sooner.'
